items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen rapid adoption in social science research, particularly for zero-shot classification tasks within Computational Social Sciences (CSS). Despite documented algorithmic biases, researchers increasingly rely on these models due to their cost-efficiency in terms of time, energy, and budget. Consequently, this reliance introduces significant risks to the validity and reliability of research outcomes. Recent literature has highlighted that LLMs are not neutral agents but are deeply embedded with the socio-political values of their development environments. While U.S.-based models often reflect Western norms, emerging Chinese architectures have been shown to incorporate 'safety alignments' that prioritize geopolitical and state-aligned discourse [Ziems et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2023]. In addition, LLM decision-making is prone to the Halo Effect, where positive emotional valence can systematically inflate a model's assessment of unrelated attributes [Kim et al., 2025]. This study builds upon the framework of 'Algorithmic Alignment' to investigate how these biases manifest in zero-shot labeling tasks involving sensitive geopolitical entities using six LLMs-originating from the United States and China-with parameter counts ranging from 8B to 32B.</jats:p>
title: Decision Drivers of LLMs on Zero-Shot Classification

items.abstract: <jats:p>Recently large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT have shown impressive performance on many natural language processing tasks with zero-shot. In this work, we investigate the effectiveness of zero-shot LLMs in the financial domain. It compares the performance of ChatGPT in zero-shot mode with fine-tuned RoBERTa with annotated data, while also evaluating it against other open-source generative LLMs. The study addresses three research questions on data annotation, performance gaps, and the feasibility of employing generative models. The findings demonstrate that ChatGPT performs impressively without labeled data, but fine-tuned models generally outperform it. The research highlights the time-intensive nature of annotating with generative models.</jats:p>
title: Zero is Not Hero Yet: Benchmarking Zero-Shot Performance of LLMs for Financial Tasks
